title: Stages of the writing process
blurb: Put the five stages in order, match any writing task to its stage, and never mix up revising with editing.
question: A nursing applicant has finished a full draft of her admission essay. She moves her strongest story to the opening paragraph, then fixes a comma splice in the conclusion. Which stage of the writing process does each action belong to?

teach.body: Formally, the writing process is the sequence of stages a writer moves through to produce a finished text: prewriting, drafting, revising, editing (with proofreading), and publishing. In plain English: plan it, write it, improve the ideas, fix the language, then share it. The order matters on the TEAS, but the process is recursive: a writer can loop back to an earlier stage at any time, for example returning to research while revising.

steps.label: Publishing
steps.sub: Submit or present the final copy

teach.caption: Order items on the TEAS follow this sequence. Proofreading is the last part of editing.

teach.body: Prewriting comes before any full sentences. The writer identifies the purpose (inform, persuade, explain) and the audience, chooses and narrows the topic, generates ideas, researches, and organizes the ideas into an outline. A working thesis is drafted here too. Two jobs live side by side: generating ideas, which is loose and unjudged, and organizing them, which puts them in a logical order. Outlining is organizing, so it belongs to prewriting, not after the draft.

children.label: Questioning
children.sub: who, what, when, where, why, how

teach.caption: Listing is another idea generator: a quick column of words or phrases with no links between them.
Revising = content and organization. Editing = correctness of the language.

teach.body: Jasmine Ortiz is applying to an ADN program. She lists every memory of caring for her grandmother (prewriting), groups them into an outline (prewriting), and writes the whole essay in one evening (drafting). Next day she moves her strongest story to the opening and cuts a paragraph about her summer job (revising). Then she fixes a comma splice and the misspelling 'recieve' (editing), reads it aloud for typos (proofreading), and uploads it to the portal (publishing).

teach.text: The TEAS loves two swaps. First, revising and editing: fixing commas or spelling is EDITING, not revising, even though people say 'revise' casually. Second, outlining: it is a PREWRITING step that organizes ideas before the draft. Brainstorming is not outlining either: brainstorming produces ideas, outlining arranges them into a hierarchy.

items: Order: prewriting, drafting, revising, editing and proofreading, publishing.
Prewriting: purpose, audience, narrowed topic, idea generation, research, outline, working thesis.
Drafting: get the ideas into sentences and paragraphs; content over perfection.
Revising changes content and organization; editing fixes grammar, punctuation and spelling.
The process is recursive: writers may loop back to earlier stages.

summary: You can now list the five stages of the writing process in order and place any writing task in its correct stage. You can also separate revising (content and organization) from editing (correct language) and recognize each prewriting strategy.

A.q: Malik sets a timer for ten minutes and writes nonstop about his topic, ignoring spelling and never pausing to reread. Which prewriting strategy is he using?
A.why: Freewriting means writing continuously for a set time without stopping to correct or judge, so ideas flow onto the page.

whyNot.1: Clustering places the topic in a center bubble and links related ideas to it; it is a map, not continuous sentences.
whyNot.2: Outlining organizes ideas into a hierarchy (I., A., 1., a.); Malik is generating, not organizing.
whyNot.3: Listing jots words or short phrases in a column; Malik writes continuous sentences for a set time.

A.q: Which task belongs to the revising stage of the writing process?
options: Fixing a misspelled word in paragraph two
Adding a missing comma after an introductory clause
Moving paragraph three to follow paragraph one
Listing ideas on the topic before writing
A.why: Revising improves content and organization. Rearranging paragraphs so the ideas build logically is a revising task.

whyNot.0: Correcting spelling is editing: it fixes the correctness of the language, not the content.
whyNot.1: Adding a comma is a punctuation fix, which is editing.
whyNot.3: Listing ideas before writing is a prewriting strategy.

A.q: Which sequence shows the stages of the writing process in the correct order?
A.why: The standard order is prewriting, drafting, revising, editing (including proofreading) and publishing: plan, write, improve the ideas, fix the language, share.

whyNot.0: Editing is placed before revising. Writers fix the big picture first so they do not polish sentences that later get cut.
whyNot.1: Drafting cannot come before prewriting: the plan comes first.
whyNot.3: Revising cannot come before drafting, because there is no draft to revise yet.

B.q: Before writing a letter to the editor about evening clinic hours, Denise asks herself who will read the newspaper and what she wants those readers to do. What is Denise doing?
options: Prewriting: arranging points into an outline
Revising: adjusting word choice for readers
Drafting: putting her ideas into sentences
B.why: Identifying who the readers are (audience) and what the writing should achieve (purpose) is the first job of prewriting.

whyNot.1: She has not arranged any points yet; she is deciding who she is writing for and why.
whyNot.2: Revising needs an existing draft, and Denise has not started writing.
whyNot.3: She is thinking about readers and goals, not writing sentences.

B.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes revising from editing?
options: Revising fixes grammar; editing reorganizes ideas
Revising improves content; editing fixes correctness
Revising checks spelling; editing adds supporting detail
Revising comes after editing and proofreading
B.why: Revising deals with what you say and how it is organized; editing deals with the correctness of the language: grammar, usage, punctuation and spelling.

whyNot.0: This swaps the two stages: grammar is editing, and reorganizing ideas is revising.
whyNot.2: Also swapped: spelling is an editing job, and adding support is a revising job.
whyNot.3: Revising comes before editing, so the writer does not polish sentences that may be cut.

B.q: Terrell writes 'sleep' in a circle in the middle of a page, then draws lines to smaller circles labeled 'shift work,' 'caffeine' and 'screens.' Which strategy is he using?
B.why: Clustering (mind mapping) puts the topic in a central bubble and links related ideas to it, showing how they connect.

whyNot.0: Outlining arranges ideas in a numbered and lettered hierarchy, not in linked bubbles.
whyNot.1: Freewriting is nonstop writing in sentences for a set time.
whyNot.2: Listing writes ideas in a plain column with no links drawn between them.

C.q: Jordan has a complete draft of his scholarship essay. His advisor says the second paragraph wanders off topic and the conclusion adds a new idea that is never supported. What should Jordan do next?
options: Edit the sentences for comma errors
Return to prewriting for a new topic
Proofread for typos and then publish
C.why: Off-topic material and an unsupported idea are content and organization problems, so the next step is revising: delete what does not belong and fix the ending.

whyNot.0: Commas are an editing issue; fixing them leaves the off-topic paragraph in place.
whyNot.2: The topic itself is not the problem, so starting over is unnecessary; the process is recursive, but this draft needs revising.
whyNot.3: Proofreading catches surface slips; publishing now would submit the content problems.

C.q: Which statement about the writing process is accurate?
options: Outlining normally takes place after the first draft
Brainstorming arranges ideas into a formal hierarchy
Proofreading focuses on the order of the paragraphs
Writers may return to an earlier stage as they work
C.why: The writing process is recursive: a writer can loop back, for example returning to research while revising.

whyNot.0: Outlining is a prewriting step that organizes ideas before drafting.
whyNot.1: Brainstorming generates ideas without judging them; arranging them into a hierarchy is outlining.
whyNot.2: Paragraph order is a revising concern; proofreading is the final check for typos and surface errors.

C.q: Priya did these tasks for a health-science report: (1) fixed a subject-verb agreement error, (2) jotted down every idea she had about hand hygiene, (3) wrote the full report from her notes, (4) added a statistic to support her second point. In what order should they happen?
C.why: Jotting ideas is prewriting (2), writing the report is drafting (3), adding support is revising (4), and fixing agreement is editing (1).

whyNot.1: This edits (1) before revising (4); content changes should come before sentence-level fixes.
whyNot.2: This drafts (3) before prewriting (2); ideas are generated before the draft.
whyNot.3: This adds support (4) before there is a draft (3) to support it.

reteach.title: Writing is like cooking for guests
reteach.question: Picture cooking a dinner for friends. Which kitchen job matches each stage of writing?

blocks.body: First you plan the menu: who is coming, what they like, what you need to buy (prewriting: audience, purpose, research, outline). Then you cook everything (drafting). You taste and adjust: add a side dish, drop one that does not fit (revising, the big changes). Then you wipe the plate edges and fix the garnish (editing and proofreading, the small fixes). Finally you serve (publishing).

blocks.text: Changing WHAT is on the plate is revising. Tidying HOW it looks is editing. If a task changes the ideas, it is revising; if it fixes the language, it is editing.

explain.body: Plan before writing: identify purpose and audience, narrow the topic, generate ideas (brainstorming, freewriting, listing, clustering, questioning), research, outline and draft a working thesis.

test.q: Which prewriting strategy generates ideas by asking who, what, when, where, why and how about a topic?
test.why: Questioning uses the reporter's questions (who, what, when, where, why, how) to open up a topic.

whyNot.0: Clustering links ideas in bubbles around a central topic.
whyNot.2: Outlining organizes ideas that already exist into a hierarchy.
whyNot.3: Freewriting is nonstop writing without planned questions.

explain.body: Turn the plan into sentences and paragraphs. The focus is content, not perfection: get the ideas down in order, following the outline, and leave polishing for later stages.

test.q: During the drafting stage, what should a writer focus on most?
options: Perfect spelling and punctuation in each line
Turning the plan into sentences and paragraphs
Narrowing the topic and identifying the audience
Checking the final copy for typing mistakes
test.why: Drafting means writing the planned ideas in sentences and paragraphs; content comes before perfection.

whyNot.0: Correct spelling and punctuation is the job of editing, after revising.
whyNot.2: Narrowing the topic and identifying the audience happen in prewriting.
whyNot.3: Checking the final copy for typos is proofreading, the last check before publishing.

explain.body: Revising changes content and organization: add, rearrange, remove or replace ideas, sharpen the thesis, improve transitions. Editing fixes sentence-level correctness: grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling and consistency.

test.q: Kenji deletes a sentence that does not support his thesis and moves his strongest example to the start of the paragraph. Which stage is he working in?
test.why: Deleting irrelevant material and rearranging ideas change content and organization, which is revising.

whyNot.0: Editing fixes grammar, punctuation and spelling, not which ideas stay or where they go.
whyNot.1: Proofreading is the final check for typos and surface errors.
whyNot.3: Drafting produces the first full version; Kenji is improving a draft that already exists.

explain.body: Proofreading is the final pass for surface errors such as typos and doubled words, often treated as the last part of editing. Publishing is submitting or presenting the final copy.

test.q: Which task is the final check a writer makes just before a paper is submitted?
test.why: Proofreading is the final check for surface errors and typos before publishing.

whyNot.0: Revising the thesis is a big-picture change that comes well before the final check.
whyNot.1: Outlining is a prewriting step that organizes ideas before drafting.
